Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
- 27-year-old man evaluated via video consult for mild local reaction and concern about possible anaphylaxis minutes after a bee/wasp sting.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Rash at sting site (right arm) with mild soreness; subjective mild shortness of breath and mild right-sided lip tingling/swelling minutes after sting.
- Onset/duration: Sting occurred “a few minutes ago” before call; symptoms present since.
- Associated symptoms: No objective breathing compromise, no stridor, no throat swelling on video; tongue “feels weird”; anxious.
- Pertinent negatives: No previous anaphylaxis; no EpiPen; no food/pet allergies; no known respiratory disease.
- Past medical history: Eczema; occasional anxiety attacks.
- Allergies: Penicillin.
- Medications: None; no antihistamines taken yet.
- Social / preventive: Lives alone; works as computer scientist; owns a cat; no other social history provided.

Examination:
- Vitals: Not documented.
- General: Conversing in full sentences, no respiratory distress observed.
- Mouth/throat: No visible lip or oropharyngeal swelling; airway appears patent.
- Skin (arm): Small puncture mark with mild redness/blotchy rash; no obvious swelling or heat.
- Cardiopulmonary: Breathing appears normal on video (no wheeze/stridor).

Impression:
- Localized allergic reaction to bee/wasp sting; low likelihood of evolving anaphylaxis at present.

Plan:
- Start oral antihistamine (e.g., Piriton/Chlorphenamine 4 mg, dose/route/frequency not documented, up to six times daily, or once-daily non-sedating alternative) – OTC purchase advised.
- Education on red-flag symptoms: lip/tongue or facial swelling, breathing difficulty, stridor, spreading rash, signs of infection; seek emergency care (A&E) immediately if these develop.
- Safety-net for rash: If erythema spreads, becomes hot, or painful, consult GP for possible antibiotics.
- Provide patient information link on anaphylaxis.
- No allergy testing indicated unless reactions become recurrent.
- Follow-up: PRN; lower threshold to re-contact if concerned.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: Vitals, complete medication list/reconciliation beyond current “none,” alcohol/tobacco history.
● Internal conflicts: Patient reported breathing difficulty and lip swelling; clinician observed none – conflict noted and explained in assessment.
● Transcript quality: Clear; minor conversational interruptions but clinically adequate.
